title: TypeScript for AI Applications
subtitle: Python trains the model. TypeScript ships the product.

slides.title: Why this track exists
bullets: Once the model is an HTTP call, the product language is what matters
The application layer is streaming, tools, cancellation, and the edge
One lesson underneath everything: types do not exist at runtime
Target: ship a streaming chat route that survives a hostile model
slides.notes: Set the frame early. This is not a TypeScript tutorial; it is the engineering of the layer between a model endpoint and a user.

slides.title: The division of labour
bullets: Python: data prep, training, eval, a model behind an HTTP API
TypeScript: routes, tool execution, streaming, auth, quotas, the UI
The contract between them is JSON over HTTPS -- that is all
Do NOT rewrite your eval harness or data pipeline in TypeScript
slides.notes: The last bullet is the honest counter-argument. The Python ecosystem gap for training and evals is not closing.

slides.title: Why TypeScript won this layer
rows: one Message type, no codegen, no drift
ReadableStream and async iterators are platform APIs
Workers, Vercel Edge, Deno Deploy, Bun
one Zod schema = validator + type + JSON Schema
not ports; the types encode the real API shape
slides.notes: Row 4 is the one people underrate. Three artifacts from one declaration is the whole pitch for Zod.

slides.title: Discriminated unions carry everything
bullets: Almost every LLM API object is a tagged union on a 'type' field
Content blocks: text | thinking | tool_use | tool_result
Stream events: message_start | content_block_delta | error | ...
Narrowing on the discriminant gives you the right member for free
Stop writing your own ChatMessage -- import the SDK's types
slides.notes: A hand-rolled { role: string; content: unknown } is strictly worse than Anthropic.MessageParam. It loses the literal union and the block discrimination.

slides.title: Exhaustiveness checking: five lines that pay rent
bullets: function assertNever(x: never): never { throw new Error(...) }
Put it in the default case of every switch over a union
Providers ADD stream event types -- your build should fail, not your UI
Without it, a 'default: break' silently drops a whole feature
Pair with noFallthroughCasesInSwitch
slides.notes: This is the highest-leverage five lines in an AI codebase. Demo it live: add a union member, watch tsc name the case you forgot.

slides.title: The central fact
slides.quote: A TypeScript type does not exist at runtime. The model has never seen your tsconfig.
bullets: tsc cannot check a network response
Structured outputs reduce the odds; they do not remove them
In the lab demo, 3 of 5 tool calls from a 'good' model were malformed
Compile-time types describe intent. Only a validator enforces it
slides.notes: Run code/typed-tool-calling.ts on screen here. The score card slide at the end of that script sells the point better than any argument.

slides.title: Zod: one declaration, three artifacts
bullets: z.infer<typeof S>            -> the static type
S.safeParse(modelOutput)     -> the runtime check
z.toJSONSchema(S, {io:'input'}) -> what you send the model
The alternative is three files that silently drift apart
Nothing links a hand-written schema to a hand-written interface
slides.notes: Emphasise that the JSON Schema is DERIVED. The number one cause of bad tool calls is a schema that no longer matches the validator.

slides.title: Zod rules for model-facing schemas
rows: a throw is a dead turn in an agent loop
becomes the JSON Schema description; cheapest accuracy win
models emit explicit null better than they omit keys
defaults change which fields are required
models usually self-repair on the next turn
slides.notes: Row 4 is subtle: a field with .default() is optional on input and always present on output. Get it backwards and you lie to the model.

slides.title: Gotcha: zod-to-json-schema on Zod v4
bullets: Zod v4 ships z.toJSONSchema() natively -- use it
Point the old package at a v4 schema and it does NOT throw
It reads v3 internals, finds nothing, and returns {}
An empty schema = zero constraints = the model invents fields
Silent in dev, loud in prod. Keep the package only if pinned to v3
slides.notes: Section 2 of typed-tool-calling.ts prints the empty definitions object. Show it. This class of silent-degradation bug is the worst kind.

slides.title: Streaming is a product requirement
bullets: Time-to-first-token is what users feel; total latency is what dashboards show
600 tokens is 8-20 seconds of spinner without it
Streaming is also your only cancellation point
A non-streaming request bills you even after the user leaves
Three layers: SSE framing, event semantics, your own UI transport
slides.notes: Transition into streaming here. You should almost never write layer 1 -- the SDK does it. Write it only when proxying and re-framing, or debugging someone else's parser. Ask who has written an SSE parser, then ask if they tested it at one-byte chunks.

slides.title: The five streaming bugs, in order
rows: accented chars and emoji become U+FFFD
Split on blank line, drop rest
decode() with no args, drain buffer
half a sentence, HTTP 200, no log
slides.notes: Bugs 1 to 3 are one bug in three hats: chunk boundaries are not message boundaries. TCP knows nothing about SSE frames or code points.

slides.title: Why these bugs ship
slides.quote: On localhost the whole response arrives in one 4KB read, so every test passes.
bullets: A CDN, a proxy, or a slow mobile link slices it anywhere
The naive parser is correct at 4096 bytes and empty at 7 bytes
Test your parser at chunkBytes = 1. If it passes there, it passes anywhere
Record one real SSE response and replay it at five chunk sizes
slides.notes: The recorded-fixture replay test is the highest-value test in an AI codebase and almost nobody writes it.

slides.title: Cancellation, end to end
bullets: Stop button -> client AbortController -> connection closes
-> server Request.signal -> provider request aborted -> billing stops
Every link must be connected or you have a decorative Stop button
Treat AbortError as normal control flow, not a 500
Breaking a 'for await' loop calls return() and cleans up for you
slides.notes: Backpressure comes free from await in a for-await loop, and from pull() in a ReadableStream. Pushing everything in start() reinvents an unbounded buffer.

slides.title: Three SDKs, three jobs
rows: building a chat product, want portability
coding or filesystem agent, tools included
slides.notes: Do not confuse the Agent SDK with the API SDK's beta tool runner. The tool runner loops over tools YOU define and has no built-in tools.

slides.title: AI SDK: the line that earns its keep
bullets: streamText({ model, messages, tools }) with Zod inputSchema per tool
return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse()
useChat() on the client already speaks that protocol
generateObject / streamObject give you validated typed output
v5 renamed a lot -- check ai-sdk.dev before trusting any snippet
slides.notes: maxTokens became maxOutputTokens, CoreMessage became ModelMessage, toDataStreamResponse became toUIMessageStreamResponse, hooks moved to @ai-sdk/react.

slides.title: Runtimes
rows: fast installs and startup, TS native
V8 isolate, no fs, CPU caps
slides.notes: Opinion: run the streaming chat route at the edge where TTFT matters, keep the agent loop and anything touching a filesystem on Node.

slides.title: What actually breaks on the edge
bullets: No filesystem: no fs, no __dirname, no path-based asset loading
Node built-ins are opt-in (nodejs_compat); net and child_process never work
CPU time is capped; waiting on a stream is I/O, so that part is fine
Response duration limits: a 10-minute agent run is not a request handler
Background work must use waitUntil() or it is killed with the response
slides.notes: The floating-promise-for-logging pattern is the most common edge bug. It works in dev and silently drops your analytics in production.

slides.title: The tsconfig flags that actually matter
rows: table stakes, not a finish line
arr[0] is T|undefined -- the empty-content case
missing vs null; providers treat them differently
forces import type; kills ESM/CJS surprises
slides.notes: Turn them on one at a time on an existing codebase and count how many new errors were real bugs. That is exercise 6 in the lab.

slides.title: Toolchain, and the mistake everyone makes
bullets: pnpm for installs, vitest for tests, biome for lint and format
Go ESM-only: 'type': 'module', no dual build, no three-day tax
tsx and esbuild DO NOT typecheck -- they strip types and run
If tsc --noEmit is not in CI, you do not have types, you have comments
Test parsers and schemas offline; run live evals on a schedule, not in CI
slides.notes: The tsx bullet is the one to dwell on. People ship type errors for months because the app runs fine locally.

slides.title: Your exit check
bullets: A POST /api/chat that streams SSE and validates input with Zod
One Zod tool; bad arguments return tool_result is_error, never a throw
Client disconnect aborts the provider call and logs 'cancelled'
Clean under strict + noUncheckedIndexedAccess + exactOptionalPropertyTypes
A test replaying a recorded SSE fixture at 1-byte and 4096-byte chunks
slides.notes: If the last bullet passes, they have beaten the bug that ships in most AI products. Point them at lab/EXERCISES.md and the python sibling track.
